passages.happening:
“This month is the beginning of months for you; it shall be the first month of your year” (verse 2). On the tenth day “each man must select a lamb for his family, one per household” (verse 3). A small household is to share with its nearest neighbor (verse 4). The lamb must be “an unblemished year-old male, and you may take it from the sheep or the goats” (verse 5).

On the fourteenth day, at twilight, they are to kill it. “They are to take some of the blood and put it on the sides and tops of the doorframes of the houses where they eat the lambs” (verse 7). They eat the meat that night, “roasted over the fire, along with unleavened bread and bitter herbs” (verse 8).

“You must be fully dressed for travel, with your sandals on your feet and your staff in your hand. You are to eat in haste; it is the LORD’s Passover” (verse 11).

“On that night I will pass through the land of Egypt and strike down every firstborn male, both man and beast, and I will execute judgment against all the gods of Egypt. I am the LORD. The blood on the houses where you are staying will distinguish them; when I see the blood, I will pass over you” (verses 12-13).
passages.hearers:
Everything in Exodus so far has been leading to this night. In several earlier plagues God set Israel apart without their doing anything (8:22; 9:26). This time protection comes through a lamb, its blood, and a meal eaten in obedience.

The first command God gives Israel as a people is about time. ‘This month is the beginning of months.’ Israel's year will begin with its rescue. The month was called Abib, a word linked with fresh ears of grain, in the spring. After the exile in Babylon it came to be called Nisan. Since the month began at the new moon, the fourteenth fell at the full moon. The night of the Passover was a moonlit night.

It is a household meal. Each family takes a lamb or a young goat; the Hebrew word covers both. It must be a year-old male without a flaw, the best of the flock, not what was left over. It is kept four days, killed at twilight, roasted whole over the fire, and eaten that night. Anything left over is burned.

The bread is unleavened, made without the bit of old fermented dough kept back to make new dough rise. The herbs are bitter. The text does not say which herbs; the Mishnah lists lettuce, chicory and others like them. Later tradition read them as a taste of slavery, since 1:14 says the Egyptians made Israel's lives bitter, using the same Hebrew root.

The blood goes on the sides and top of the doorframe, the frame every person entering must pass through. ‘Passover’, Pesach in Hebrew, comes from the verb in verse 13: God will ‘pass over’ the marked houses. The blood does not work like magic. It protects because God promised that he would see it.

And they eat dressed for the road, sandals on, staff in hand, ready to walk out before morning. God's judgment falls not only on Egypt's firstborn but on ‘all the gods of Egypt’. The powers Egypt trusted are shown to be no gods.
passages.later:
Joshua's people kept the Passover when they first entered the land: “On the evening of the fourteenth day of the month, while the Israelites were camped at Gilgal on the plains of Jericho, they kept the Passover” (Joshua 5:10).

The New Testament reads Jesus' death through this night more than through any other in Exodus. John the Baptist says, “Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29). Paul writes, “For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7). Peter speaks of believers redeemed “with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot” (1 Peter 1:19), echoing verse 5.
passages.hard:
What did the Passover blood mean, and where did the rite come from?

Some critical scholars argue that the Passover is older than the exodus story. One proposal, from the 1940s, compared the customs of later herding peoples and suggested that it began as a shepherds' rite at the spring move to new pasture, with blood smeared on the tent door to ward off harm, and that Israel later joined it to the story of the exodus. Many scholars now judge that reconstruction too speculative, and others have proposed different backgrounds, so its prehistory is uncertain. Those who read the chapter as telling how the rite began see no need for an earlier background. And even those who accept one note that Exodus gives the rite an entirely new meaning: the blood protects because God has promised to see it (verse 13), and the destroyer acts only under God's command (verse 23).

On the meaning of the blood, readers differ. Many Christian interpreters, and some Jewish ones, see a substitute: Israel's firstborn were spared not because they were better than Egyptians but because a lamb had died in the house. Leviticus later states the principle for all sacrificial blood: “it is the blood that makes atonement for the soul” (Leviticus 17:11). Others, among them many Jewish commentators and some Christians, stress that the Passover is not a sin offering but a protecting meal that marks out God's people, whose heart is rescue and belonging. An old Jewish commentary on Exodus, the Mekhilta, reads the blood of the Passover beside the blood of circumcision as Israel's first acts of obedience. The text supports both: it calls the rite a sacrifice (verse 27), and it centers it on a family meal. These notes do not choose between them.
passages.asks: Israel was spared not because they were better, but because God promised to see the blood. Ask what it means to you to be safe because of what God provides, and not because of what you have earned. And ask whether you are living, like Israel that night, ready to follow God when he calls.

passages.happening:
“And this day will be a memorial for you, and you are to celebrate it as a feast to the LORD, as a permanent statute for the generations to come” (verse 14).

“For seven days you must eat unleavened bread. On the first day you are to remove the leaven from your houses” (verse 15). The first and seventh days are days of sacred assembly, with no work but preparing food (verse 16).

“So you are to keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread, for on this very day I brought your divisions out of the land of Egypt” (verse 17). It runs “from the evening of the fourteenth day until the evening of the twenty-first day” (verse 18), for foreigner and native alike (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
Before the night has even happened, God gives the rules for remembering it. The event is told so that it can be kept. The phrase ‘for the generations to come’ comes back again and again in this chapter.

Leaven was a lump of fermented dough kept back from an earlier batch to make the next batch rise. Removing all of it from the house meant a fresh start. This is the origin of the Jewish custom, still kept, of searching the house for leaven by lamplight on the night before Passover.

Seven days of unleavened bread recalls the haste of the leaving. There was no time to let bread rise.

Notice that the feast is for foreigners living among Israel as well as for those born Israelites (verse 19). The door is not shut.

Passover is not only a feast in an old book. Jewish families still keep it today. After the temple in Jerusalem was destroyed in AD 70, lambs could no longer be sacrificed, and the Seder became the Jewish form of the feast: four cups of wine, the children's questions, and a retelling that begins in shame and ends in praise. A roasted bone on the Seder plate recalls the lamb. The Samaritans, a small community who hold Mount Gerizim to be God's chosen place, still sacrifice Passover lambs there each year. Christians should speak of these living observances with respect. Passover is the Jewish people's own remembrance of what God did for them, and it still is.
passages.later:
Deuteronomy calls the unleavened loaves “the bread of affliction, because you left the land of Egypt in haste” (Deuteronomy 16:3).

Paul takes up the picture of clearing out the leaven: “Get rid of the old leaven, that you may be a new unleavened batch, as you really are. For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7). He does not take the feast away from Israel. He uses its picture to call the church to a clean life: “Therefore let us keep the feast, not with the old bread, leavened with malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and of truth” (1 Corinthians 5:8).
passages.asks: God gave the rules for remembering before the rescue had even happened. Ask what God has done for you that you are in danger of forgetting. And ask what simple habit could help you, and those you love, remember it year by year.

passages.t: ‘What does this service mean to you?’
passages.happening:
Moses calls the elders: “Go at once and select for yourselves a lamb for each family, and slaughter the Passover lamb. Take a cluster of hyssop, dip it into the blood in the basin, and brush the blood on the top and sides of the doorframe. None of you shall go out the door of his house until morning” (verses 21-22).

When the LORD passes through, he will see the blood “and will pass over that doorway; so He will not allow the destroyer to enter your houses and strike you down” (verse 23).

“When your children ask you, ‘What does this service mean to you?’ you are to reply, ‘It is the Passover sacrifice to the LORD, who passed over the houses of the Israelites in Egypt when He struck down the Egyptians and spared our homes’” (verses 26-27). “Then the people bowed down and worshiped. And the Israelites went and did just what the LORD had commanded Moses and Aaron” (verses 27-28).
passages.hearers:
Hyssop was a small bushy plant, usually identified with a kind of marjoram, whose hairy stems hold liquid well. It was used for sprinkling in rites of cleansing.

The word for doorpost, mezuzah, later gave its name to the small case holding verses of Scripture that Jewish families fix to their doorframes.

‘None of you shall go out.’ Safety is inside, under the blood, all night. And ‘the destroyer’ acts only as God allows.

Then the children's question. It is one of four such questions in the Torah (12:26; 13:8, 14; Deuteronomy 6:20). The Passover Haggadah, the order of the Jewish Passover meal, builds its teaching of four kinds of children on them. The feast is built so that children ask and parents tell.

‘This service’ uses the same Hebrew word as Israel's slave labor in Egypt. The word for slavery has become the word for worship.

And verse 28 says Israel obeyed before anything had happened. Pharaoh refused ten times. Israel obeys at once, on God's word alone.
passages.later:
Israel's later law repeats the children's question: “In the future, when your son asks, ‘What is the meaning of the decrees and statutes and ordinances that the LORD our God has commanded you?’” (Deuteronomy 6:20). And the next chapter gives the answer a parent is to give: “This is because of what the LORD did for me when I came out of Egypt” (Exodus 13:8).

A psalm prays with the same plant: “Purify me with hyssop, and I will be clean” (Psalm 51:7). At the cross, John notes, a sponge of sour wine was lifted to Jesus “on a stalk of hyssop” (John 19:29).
passages.asks: The children asked, ‘What does this mean?’ and the parents told the story. Ask whether the young people near you have ever asked you what your faith means. And ask whether you could answer simply, with what God has done for you.

passages.happening:
“Now at midnight the LORD struck down every firstborn male in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh, who sat on his throne, to the firstborn of the prisoner in the dungeon, as well as all the firstborn among the livestock” (verse 29).

Pharaoh gets up in the night, with all his officials and all Egypt, “and there was loud wailing in Egypt; for there was no house without someone dead” (verse 30).

He calls Moses and Aaron: “Get up, leave my people, both you and the Israelites! Go, worship the LORD as you have requested. Take your flocks and herds as well, just as you have said, and depart! And bless me also” (verses 31-32).

The Egyptians urge the people to hurry: “For otherwise,” they said, “we are all going to die!” (verse 33). The people take their dough before it rises (verse 34). They ask the Egyptians for silver, gold and clothing, “And the LORD gave the people such favor in the sight of the Egyptians that they granted their request” (verse 36).
passages.hearers:
The night God warned of comes. The text tells it in very few words, and it does not linger. The death of the firstborn reaches from the palace to the prison.

‘Loud wailing’ uses the same word as the cry of Israel under slavery, the cry God heard (3:7). Now Egypt cries.

Pharaoh, who once asked, ‘Who is the LORD?’ (5:2), now says, ‘Go, worship the LORD’. Every condition he tried to set is gone: the children, the flocks, all of it. And then a strange last request: ‘bless me also’. The king who would not let God's people go now asks them for a blessing.

The Egyptians themselves press Israel to leave. There is no time to let the bread rise. The dough is carried out in kneading bowls wrapped in cloaks.

No Egyptian text mentions the death of the firstborn or Israel's leaving. Historians weigh that silence differently. Some treat the exodus as a later national epic. Others argue that the Egyptian background of the story is genuine and early, and that Egyptian royal records rarely recorded defeats. The book page sets out these views.
passages.later:
Psalm 105 remembers this night: “Then He struck all the firstborn in their land, the firstfruits of all their vigor” (Psalm 105:36). Hebrews says that Moses “kept the Passover and the sprinkling of blood, so that the destroyer of the firstborn would not touch Israel’s own firstborn” (Hebrews 11:28).

The New Testament speaks of God doing the reverse of what he did that night. He did not take the firstborn of his enemies but gave his own Son: “He who did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all” (Romans 8:32).
passages.hard:
How could a just God kill the firstborn of Egypt, from Pharaoh's heir to the prisoner's son? The question should be stated fully. The verse describes the death of every firstborn son in Egypt, including children and prisoners who had no part in Pharaoh's decisions, and even animals. Many readers, not only hostile ones, find it the hardest verse in the book.

Several answers are given, usually together. First, the judgment answers a crime. Pharaoh had ordered every Hebrew boy thrown into the Nile (1:22), and God warned him at the start that because he would not release God's firstborn son, Israel, his own firstborn would die (4:22-23). Nine plagues and many chances to relent came first. Second, the blow is aimed at Egypt's gods and its god-king (verse 12): Pharaoh's heir was the next king, thought divine. Third, Israel was not exempt by nature. Its firstborn were spared only under the blood, and afterward God claimed them and they were redeemed (13:1-2, 13). That suggests the judgment is one all deserve and from which all need rescue. Fourth, Scripture holds that God, who gives life, has the right to take it (Deuteronomy 32:39). Christians add that the God of Exodus finally gives his own Son rather than taking the sons of others.

None of these answers makes the verse easy. Some thoughtful Christians, while confessing that God is just, admit that it remains a place where they must trust what they cannot fully see. Jewish tradition felt the weight early. The Talmud tells that God silenced the angels who wanted to sing as the Egyptians drowned, saying that the work of his hands was dying, and the Passover custom of spilling wine as the plagues are named has often been explained as lessening joy at an enemy's suffering. Israel remembers this night with thanks and with grief.

Behind every one of those Egyptian doors was a mother. If you have lost a child, or carry a grief like hers, please do not carry it alone. Speak to someone you trust, a pastor or a grief counsellor, and if the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Egypt's cry that night was the same word as Israel's cry in slavery. Ask whether you can grieve even for those who did great wrong, as Jewish tradition grieves for Egypt. And ask what it means to you that God heard both cries.

passages.t: From Rameses to Succoth, after 430 years
passages.happening:
The Israelites set out “from Rameses to Succoth with about 600,000 men on foot, besides women and children” (verse 37). “And a mixed multitude also went up with them, along with great droves of livestock” (verse 38). They bake unleavened loaves from the dough they carried, because “they could not delay” (verse 39).

“Now the duration of the Israelites’ stay in Egypt was 430 years. At the end of the 430 years, to the very day, all the LORD’s divisions went out of the land of Egypt” (verses 40-41).

“Because the LORD kept a vigil that night to bring them out of the land of Egypt, this same night is to be a vigil to the LORD, to be observed by all the Israelites for the generations to come” (verse 42).
passages.hearers:
Rameses is the Delta city of the store cities in 1:11, usually identified with Pi-Ramesses, the capital of Ramesses II. Those who date the exodus to the 1400s take the name as an older place name brought up to date. Succoth is widely identified with a place in the Wadi Tumilat, a valley running east from the Delta toward the Bitter Lakes. The road out of Egypt begins.

‘A mixed multitude’ went with them. Not everyone who left was born an Israelite. People from other backgrounds joined God's people on the way out.

Israel leaves as ‘the LORD's divisions’, an army leaving in order, not a mob of runaways. And because the LORD ‘kept a vigil’ that night, Israel keeps it as a vigil too. The Hebrew word names both God's watching and theirs.

The 430 years are counted in more than one way. The standard Hebrew text says Israel lived in Egypt 430 years. The ancient Greek translation and the Samaritan version count from Abraham's arrival in Canaan, which would make the stay in Egypt itself about 215 years. Paul's statement that the law came 430 years after the promise to Abraham (Galatians 3:17) fits that reckoning. Those who keep the Hebrew figure point to the four hundred years of Genesis 15:13. Most textual scholars regard the Hebrew reading as original.
passages.later:
The census in Numbers gives a total of fighting men that agrees with this number: “And all those counted totaled 603,550” (Numbers 1:46).

Paul writes, “The law that came 430 years later does not revoke the covenant previously established by God” (Galatians 3:17). Stephen says Abraham's descendants “would be enslaved and mistreated four hundred years” (Acts 7:6).

The mixed multitude is a small sign of something larger. God had promised Abraham that his family would bring good to “all the families of the earth” (Genesis 12:3).
passages.hard:
How many left Egypt? ‘About 600,000 men on foot, besides women and children’ would mean, with families, two million or more.

Christians read this in more than one way. Some take the number as it stands. They note that it agrees with the census totals in Numbers (Numbers 1:46; 26:51), and that God's power is not limited by what seems likely.

Others point out that the Hebrew word elef, usually ‘thousand’, can also mean a clan or a military unit. Gideon uses the same word when he says, “my clan is the weakest in Manasseh” (Judges 6:15). Read that way, ‘600 elef’ could mean six hundred clans or units, and the company would be far smaller. Several scholars have worked out versions of this reading, among them George Mendenhall (1958) and Colin Humphreys (1998).

Each reading has its difficulty. The first must explain how so great a number fits what is known of the land and its archaeology. The second must explain why the census lists add up as if they were thousands.

Some scholars also doubt that the exodus happened on the scale Exodus describes, or think a smaller group's escape grew in the telling into the story of the whole nation. The book page sets out these views. Christians who hold Scripture as God's word are found on more than one side of the numbers, and these notes take no side. On every reading, the chapter's claim is the same: the LORD brought his people out.
passages.asks: God kept watch that night, and Israel was told to keep watch in return. Ask whether there is a night or a day in your year when you deliberately remember what God has done. And ask what it would look like to keep watch for God, as he kept watch for you.

passages.happening:
“This is the statute of the Passover: No foreigner is to eat of it. But any slave who has been purchased may eat of it, after you have circumcised him” (verses 43-44). A temporary resident or hired worker may not (verse 45).

“It must be eaten inside one house. You are not to take any of the meat outside the house, and you may not break any of the bones” (verse 46).

“If a foreigner resides with you and wants to celebrate the LORD’s Passover, all the males in the household must be circumcised; then he may come near to celebrate it, and he shall be like a native of the land” (verse 48). “The same law shall apply to both the native and the foreigner who resides among you” (verse 49).

“And on that very day the LORD brought the Israelites out of the land of Egypt by their divisions” (verse 51).
passages.hearers:
The ‘mixed multitude’ of verse 38 raises a question: who may share the meal? The answer is that the Passover belongs to those who belong to the covenant. An outsider passing through may not eat it. But the door is open. A foreigner who wants to join, and takes the sign of the covenant, ‘shall be like a native of the land’. One law for both.

Even a slave in an Israelite household could eat it, once circumcised. The text speaks of the slavery of its time without comment. These notes do not defend slavery, and the notes on Exodus 21 face the laws about slaves directly.

No bone of the lamb was to be broken. The lamb was to be kept whole.

The chapter ends as it began, with obedience and with God's act. Israel did all that God commanded. And ‘on that very day’ the LORD brought them out.
passages.later:
John sees this rule fulfilled at the cross. The soldiers did not break Jesus' legs, and John writes, “Now these things happened so that the Scripture would be fulfilled: ‘Not one of His bones will be broken’” (John 19:36). He draws on the Passover rule (and Numbers 9:12) and on a psalm: “He protects all his bones; not one of them will be broken” (Psalm 34:20).

Revelation sings of a Lamb who by his blood “purchased for God those from every tribe and tongue and people and nation” (Revelation 5:9), a people from every nation, as the Passover law already opened the meal to foreigners who wished to join.
passages.asks: The meal was for those who belonged, and anyone could come to belong. Ask whether you have thought of yourself as an outsider to God's people. And ask who around you is standing at the door, and how you might welcome them in.
